claims.text: The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy is an FCC solid solution.
Random atomic distribution in FeNiCrMn produces severe lattice distortion.
The initial material is free of pre-existing dislocations and phase transformations.
Yield strength in single-crystal FeNiCrMn is relatively insensitive to strain rate in the elastic-to-plastic transition.
The onset of yielding is dominated by thermally activated dislocation nucleation rather than an athermal mechanism or phase transformation.
Lattice distortion creates solute clusters and stacking-fault tetrahedra that obstruct dislocation nucleation and motion.
The lattice-distortion-induced obstacles impose a high energy barrier to dislocation motion.
Thermal fluctuations enable dislocations to overcome the lattice-distortion-induced barriers.
Yield strength should depend significantly on temperature.
Thermally assisted barrier crossing makes yield strength relatively insensitive to strain rate.
Dislocation accumulation increases with strain rate even though yield strength remains relatively constant.
Plastic deformation remains dominated by FCC {111}<110> slip.
Yield strength varies with crystal orientation through the Schmid factor.
A high Peierls stress caused by lattice distortion reduces the orientation anisotropy normally found in pure FCC metals.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation occurs during yielding at temperatures from 77 K to 600 K, including at high strain rates.
Traditional FCC metals such as Ni and Cu exhibit strong yield-strength strain-rate sensitivity due to athermal dislocation-motion mechanisms.
The hypothesis is limited to single crystals because grain-boundary effects may dominate in polycrystalline material.
The proposed loading matrix spans strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1, temperatures of 77 to 600 K, and [100], [110], and [111] loading orientations.
Detection of a BCC phase during yielding would falsify the claim that FCC slip, rather than FCC-to-BCC transformation, controls deformation.
Strong yield-strength strain-rate sensitivity or demonstrably athermal dislocation nucleation would falsify the proposed thermal-activation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as free of pre-existing dislocations, while stacking-fault tetrahedra—defects bounded by partial-dislocation structures—are simultaneously presented as existing obstacles responsible for yielding.
